title: Evidence & Measurement Method Plates
purpose: Live instructional plates that close the most important method-teaching gaps while dedicated downloadable infographic masters are still in artwork production.

plates.title: Accuracy, Precision, Resolution & Uncertainty
plates.coreIdea: A measurement can be repeatable without being correct, and a display can show more digits than the method can justify.

states.label: Accurate + precise
states.meaning: Repeated values cluster near the reference.

states.label: Accurate + imprecise
states.meaning: Values spread around the reference; the average may be close while individual readings vary.

states.label: Precise + biased
states.meaning: Values cluster tightly but are consistently displaced from the reference.

states.label: Imprecise + biased
states.meaning: Values are both scattered and displaced from the reference.

methodSteps: Define the measurand and unit before comparing instruments or readings.
Check the instrument specification for stated accuracy, resolution, operating range and environmental limitations.
Compare against an appropriate reference or standard when the method allows.
Repeat measurements under the same condition to estimate repeatability.
Report only digits supported by the method and preserve the uncertainty or known tolerance.
failureModes: Treating two decimal places as evidence of high accuracy.
Calling a stable offset 'good data' because the readings repeat.
Comparing values produced by different methods without documenting the method difference.
Hiding spread by reporting only an average.
plates.interpretationLimit: Repeated measurements can estimate precision, but repetition alone cannot reveal a shared systematic bias.
plates.knowledgeCheck: If a meter repeatedly reads 6.20 against a traceable 6.00 reference, is it precise, accurate, both, or neither? Explain why.

plates.title: Calibration, Drift & Reference Cross-Checks
plates.coreIdea: Calibration is part of the measurement chain. Drift, contamination, aging and handling can move a sensor away from its reference even when its display looks stable.
methodSteps: Inspect the sensor and sampling interface before calibration; contamination can invalidate the check.
Use standards and procedures appropriate to the instrument and variable being measured.
Record the pre-check result before any adjustment so drift remains visible in the history.
After adjustment, verify the reading again instead of assuming the calibration succeeded.
Periodically compare field instruments with a maintained reference under the same conditions.
failureModes: Adjusting the instrument before recording how far it had drifted.
Using expired, contaminated or temperature-inappropriate standards.
Comparing two sensors placed in different microclimates and calling the difference sensor error.
Waiting for crop symptoms before checking an instrument that controls the environment.
plates.interpretationLimit: A reference instrument also has uncertainty and maintenance requirements; cross-checking improves confidence but does not create an error-free truth source.
plates.knowledgeCheck: Why is the pre-calibration reading valuable even when the meter can be adjusted immediately?

plates.title: Sensor Placement, Canopy Grids & Representative Sampling
plates.coreIdea: Location is part of the measurement definition. Height, distance from equipment, canopy density and room position can change the value being measured.
methodSteps: Define the measurement plane and height relative to the canopy.
Create fixed coordinates that can be reused after lighting, HVAC or canopy changes.
Record raw values at each point before making a heat map or summary statistic.
Use fixed sentinel positions for trend monitoring and randomized sampling when making crop-level inferences.
Document nearby obstructions, emitters, fixtures, vents and other position-specific influences.
failureModes: Using one convenient room sensor as proof of canopy uniformity.
Moving sensor height between measurements without recording it.
Keeping only the room average and losing the raw spatial pattern.
Choosing only the most damaged or healthiest leaves for a crop-level conclusion.
plates.interpretationLimit: A grid describes the points and time sampled. Interpolation between points is a model, not an additional direct measurement.
plates.knowledgeCheck: Why can the same room average hide two very different canopy environments?

plates.title: Baseline, Control, Treatment & Position Effects
plates.coreIdea: A convincing before-after story requires knowing what the system was already doing and what happened to a comparable unit that did not receive the treatment.

positionModels: confounded: treatment all on one bench edge
blocked: compare treatments within known environmental zones

methodSteps: Define the outcome before the intervention and collect enough baseline data to see ordinary variation.
When practical, retain a comparable contemporaneous control that does not receive the treatment.
Randomize or block positions when bench edge, airflow, irrigation pressure or light overlap could influence the result.
Change one major learning variable at a time when the goal is causal learning.
If an emergency requires multiple corrections, document that causal attribution is limited.
failureModes: Calling a normal upward trend a treatment response because there was no baseline.
Comparing this cycle to last cycle while many other conditions changed.
Putting every treated plant under one fixture and every control plant under another.
Stacking light, nutrition, irrigation and climate changes and later assigning credit to one of them.
plates.interpretationLimit: Production crops are not always formal experiments. The method should match the strength of the claim: operational learning can be useful without pretending it proves a universal causal rule.
plates.knowledgeCheck: What problem occurs if all treatment plants sit nearest the HVAC supply while all control plants sit at the opposite wall?

plates.title: Standardized Imaging, Scale & Scoring Anchors
plates.coreIdea: A compelling close-up is weak evidence when identity, location, scale, lighting and the scoring rule are missing.
methodSteps: Capture a whole-plant image before the close-up so distribution remains visible.
Record the organ, tissue, node or canopy location shown.
Use neutral, repeatable lighting and avoid filters or automatic color effects when diagnostic color matters.
Include a physical scale or known magnification when size is part of the observation.
Write the visible observation separately from the suspected cause and use anchored scoring definitions.
failureModes: Diagnosing from one isolated damaged leaf with no whole-plant context.
Comparing blurple-lit and daylight images as if color is directly comparable.
Using a 1–5 score when each scorer imagines a different meaning for 3.
Overwriting or discarding the unedited original image.
plates.interpretationLimit: Standardized imaging improves comparability, but an image still records appearance rather than proving the underlying biological cause.
plates.knowledgeCheck: Why should 'interveinal yellowing on older fan leaves' be recorded separately from 'magnesium deficiency'?

plates.title: Replication, Uncertainty, Correlation & the Evidence Chain
plates.coreIdea: The strength of a conclusion depends on what was independently replicated, how variable the observations were, what alternative explanations remain and whether the result can be reproduced.

replicationExamples: 5 leaves from 1 plant = subsamples of one biological unit
1 measurement from each of 5 independent plants = biological replication at the plant level

methodSteps: Define the experimental or observational unit that receives the treatment or represents the independent biological entity.
Keep individual values so spread and unusual responses remain visible.
Distinguish technical repeats or subsamples from independent biological replicates.
Treat correlation as association until temporal order, controlled comparison and plausible mechanism support a causal interpretation.
State confidence and the next measurement that could change the conclusion.
failureModes: Counting ten leaves from one plant as ten independent plants.
Showing only group averages while hiding large individual variation.
Assuming two variables moving together means one caused the other.
Writing a high-confidence diagnosis when the measurements are inconsistent or the sample is tiny.
plates.interpretationLimit: More observations do not rescue a systematically biased design. Replication estimates repeatability only at the level that was actually replicated.
plates.knowledgeCheck: Why are five leaves measured on one plant not equivalent to one leaf measured on each of five independent plants?
